steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on LCANets++, multi-layer CNNs that use sparse coding with lateral competition, for robust audio classification. It should motivate the problem, point out what is missing in earlier LCANets, and summarize what we propose and test.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Audio signal classification, for sound recognition (SR) or sound event detection (SE), is now an active research area. One example is using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models to understand human speech words like 'yes' or 'stop', and another is classifying sound events such as 'baby cries' and 'barking'. But standard CNNs are known to be very susceptible to perturbations or adversarial attacks. Also, standard audio classification models depend a lot on large labeled datasets to perform well, and large labeled datasets can be scarce for a lot of common tasks, for example speaker identification. One approach that has been proposed for this is generating augmented samples for audio data, but data augmentation can be time-consuming and it is expensive. So it is important to develop audio classifiers that can learn robust features from limited labeled samples.

Recent studies showed that CNNs which are more similar to the primary visual cortex are more robust than standard CNNs. Based on this, previous work built CNNs where the first layer does sparse coding with the Locally Competitive Algorithm (LCA), and LCA is a biologically plausible model of the primate primary visual cortex. We call these CNNs LCANets, and they were shown to be more robust than standard CNNs on standard CV tasks. But there are two issues with this approach, which we address here. The first issue is that sparse coding models were designed to model the visual cortex, so it is not clear how they will impact CNN performance on audio classification tasks. The second issue is that these LCANets were robust to natural corruptions, but they were susceptible to white-box adversarial attacks unless the exact attack was known before hand.

- Our approach
  - multi-layer LCANets: sparse coding in multiple CNN layers -> LCANets++, trained on audio classification
  - first: experiments with different audio perturbations (e.g. background noise) vs LCANets and standard CNNs
  - more robust than SOTA models (ResNet18, standard CNN) and LCANets
  - white-box attacks: fast gradient sign attack (FGSM), projected gradient descent attack (PGD)
  - black-box attacks: evasion attack

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Audio signal classification, for sound recognition (SR) or sound event detection (SE), is now an active research area. One example is using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models to understand human speech words like 'yes' or 'stop', and another is classifying sound events such as 'baby cries' and 'barking'. But standard CNNs are known to be very susceptible to perturbations or adversarial attacks. Also, standard audio classification models depend a lot on large labeled datasets to perform well, and large labeled datasets can be scarce for a lot of common tasks, for example speaker identification. One approach that has been proposed for this is generating augmented samples for audio data, but data augmentation can be time-consuming and it is expensive. So it is important to develop audio classifiers that can learn robust features from limited labeled samples.

Recent studies showed that CNNs which are more similar to the primary visual cortex are more robust than standard CNNs. Based on this, previous work built CNNs where the first layer does sparse coding with the Locally Competitive Algorithm (LCA), and LCA is a biologically plausible model of the primate primary visual cortex. We call these CNNs LCANets, and they were shown to be more robust than standard CNNs on standard CV tasks. But there are two issues with this approach, which we address here. The first issue is that sparse coding models were designed to model the visual cortex, so it is not clear how they will impact CNN performance on audio classification tasks. The second issue is that these LCANets were robust to natural corruptions, but they were susceptible to white-box adversarial attacks unless the exact attack was known before hand.

Because of this, we introduce multi-layer LCANets, which do sparse coding in multiple CNN layers. We call these multilayer LCANets LCANets++ and we train them on audio classification tasks. To test how robust LCANets++ are compared to LCANets and standard CNNs, we first ran experiments with different audio perturbations, such as background noise. We also show that our LCANets++ are more robust than the state-of-the-art (SOTA) models (e.g., ResNet18, standard CNN) and LCANets against white-box attacks, which are the fast gradient sign attack (FGSM) and the projected gradient descent attack (PGD), and also against black-box attacks, i.e., evasion attack.

Also, standard audio classification models depend a lot on large labeled datasets to perform well [7,8], and large labeled datasets can be scarce for a lot of common tasks, for example speaker identification. One approach that has been proposed for this is generating augmented samples for audio data, but data augmentation can be time-consuming and it is expensive [9,10]. So it is important to develop audio classifiers that can learn robust features from limited labeled samples.

Recent studies showed that CNNs which are more similar to the primary visual cortex are more robust than standard CNNs [11]. Based on this, previous work built CNNs where the first layer does sparse coding with the Locally Competitive Algorithm (LCA) [12,13,14], and LCA is a biologically plausible model of the primate primary visual cortex [15]. We call these CNNs LCANets, and they were shown to be more robust than standard CNNs on standard CV tasks. But there are two issues with this approach, which we address here. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Audio signal classification for the purposes of sound recognition (SR) or sound event detection (SE) has become an active area of research [1,2]. This includes using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models for understanding human speech words, e.g., 'yes', 'stop', etc., or for classifying sound events like 'baby cries' and 'barking'. However, standard CNNs are notoriously susceptible to perturbations or adversarial attacks [3,4,5,6]. Standard audio classification models also depend highly on large labeled datasets for good performance [7,8], but such datasets can be scarce for many common tasks, such as speaker identification. Generating augmented samples for audio data is one proposed way to mitigate this challenge, but data augmentation can be time-consuming and expensive [9,10]. Therefore, it is crucial to develop audio classifiers that can learn robust features with limited labeled samples.

Recent studies have shown that CNNs that are more similar to the primary visual cortex are more robust than standard CNNs [11]. Based on this, previous work developed CNNs in which the first layer performed sparse coding via the Locally Competitive Algorithm (LCA) [12,13,14], a biologically plausible model of the primate primary visual cortex [15]. These CNNs, which we refer to as LCANets, were shown to be more robust than standard CNNs on standard CV tasks. However, this approach has two issues that we address here. First, sparse coding models were designed to model the visual cortex, so it is unclear how they will impact the performance of CNNs on audio classification tasks. Second, these LCANets were robust to natural corruptions, but they were susceptible to white-box adversarial attacks [13] unless the exact attack was known before hand [14].

Motivated by this, we introduce multi-layer LCANets, which perform sparse coding in multiple CNN layers. We refer to these multilayer LCANets as LCANets++ and train them on audio classification tasks. To test the robustness of LCANets++ relative to LCANets and standard CNNs, we first conducted experiments with different audio perturbations, e.g., background noise. We also show that LCANets++ are more robust than the state-of-the-art (SOTA) models (e.g., ResNet18, standard CNN) and LCANets against white-box attacks, i.e., fast gradient sign attack (FGSM) [16] and projected gradient descent attack (PGD) [17], as well as black-box attacks, i.e., evasion attack.
